list.listitem: Current studies of mitral valve prolapse (MVP) prevalence (0.6% in adults aged 23-35 years) show substantial reductions from past surveys because of a change in diagnostic criteria. B

The most recent, and largest, meta-analysis on MVP and sudden cardiac death (SCD) shows an increased risk of SCD in MVP patients, with a hazard ratio about 2; this annual risk is nonetheless very low (< 0.2%). B
The great majority of patients with MVP will have a benign course; severe mitral regurgitation (MR) and ventricular arrhythmia risk are the best markers of risk for serious complications. B
MVP does not increase risk of stroke in patients younger than 45 years, but possibly may be associated with a mild increased lifetime risk of stroke. B
Cardiac magnetic resonance studies are superior to both echocardiography and CT in diagnosing risk for ventricular arrhtyhmias and sudden cardiac death. B
Surgery may be required for MVP with severe MR and onset of structural heart changes. B

background.definition: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is a condition in which mitral valve leaflets close above the annular plane during systole. In this circumstance, approximation of the leaflets may be inadequate and thus promote mitral regurgitation. Barlow’s Disease is a form of MVP in which the MV leaflets are thickened due to redundant tissue. Careful dissection of the MV leaflets at the time of MV repair demonstrates ruptured chordae tendineae in over 70% of thickened leaflets. Severity of MR is proportionate to the regurgitant volume, i.e., the amount of blood which flows backwards through the MV during the typical systolic cycle. The regurgitant volume is estimated by the valve area showing regurgitation, and the duration and velocity of the regurgitation. MV annular dilatation occurs with severe MR from any etiology; accordingly, severe MR from MVP is treated similarly to severe MR from other causes.

list.listitem: MVP is usually congenital with a US prevalence of 0.7% to 2.5%; the Framingham Offspring Study found a prevalence of classic MVP of 1.3% (7% with severe MR) and non-classic MVP of 1.1% (with no severe MR).
Cardiac MR criteria for MVP are now considered most accurate for yield and overall prevalence of MVP of 1-2% in adults.

Substantially higher rates of MVP (up to 38% in teenaged girls) were reported in prevalence studies in the 1980s using a different definition for the disorder. Since the mitral valve is saddle-shaped, two-dimensional (2D) echocardiograms (used in the past) can overestimate prevalence unless strict diagnostic criteria are employed. By redefining MVP as significant prolapse only in the 4-chamber view on ECHO, "classic MVP" had a prevalence of 1.3%.
Some believe that it is associated with palpitations, but this is not substantiated by studies.
Eighty percent of people in a young adult population diagnosed with MVP were unaware that they had the condition.
MVP is associated with LVH of only the basilar wall segments, with a wall thickness 1.5 to 2 times normal.
Cardiac MR studies have demonstrated that the inferior basilar myocardium and the papillary muscles are the areas of the heart most likely to experience fibrosis and risk for ventricular arrhythmia
Idiopathic/genetic .
Familial MVP (most autosomal dominant).
Secondary MVP, from MI or rheumatic injury to the valve.
Obstructive sleep apnea.
Marfan syndrome.
Ankylosing spondylitis.
Other connective tissue diseases including Lupus

Primary MVP: Proliferation of mucopolysaccharide-containing stromal tissue in the center of the valve, disrupting the strong band of collagen on the ventricular side of the valve. The valve's increased mass can stretch the chordae tendineae, cause fibrosis on the valve surface, and deposit fibrin at the angle formed by the left atrium and the mitral valve.

Secondary MVP: It arises from direct cardiac injury (e.g., papillary muscle rupture after MI causing "flail leaflet" [unchecked prolapse of one or both MV leaflets] with massive MR, or high LV pressures in OSA).

Some experts have recommended screening first-degree relatives of patients with primary MVP, but this is not recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) or American Heart Association (AHA). C
Antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent endocarditis is not recommended by the AHA for patients with MVP.
Anticoagulation is not recommended in MVP patients, unless they have had unexplained thromboembolic events.

MVP is best detected by auscultation of mid-systolic click(s) with confirmation by ECHO or cardiac MRI (gold standard).
C
Certain features of the "MVP Syndrome" (e.g., atypical chest pain, dyspnea, and anxiety) are as common in the general population as in patients with MVP. B
"Non-classic MVP" may simply be a normal variant identified by overly lax echocardiographic criteria. B

Echocardiographic criteria for "classic MVP" have been the gold standard for diagnosis, A but cardiac MRI performs better and better predicts which patients with severe MR will develop structural heart changes, necessitating MV repair.
,

Differential.Differential_Features: Lack of physical findings and normal echocardiogram
Presence of pregnancy or dehydration with "non-classic" MVP or normal echocardiogram
Lack of click, history of myocardial infarction (with papillary muscle dysfunction) or trauma

list.listitem: MVP is a clinical diagnosis (i.e., presence of click with or without a systolic murmur) and confirmed by echocardiogram or cardiac MRI.
Auscultation of a typical MR murmur is only 22.6% sensitive, but 96% specific for MVP; LR+ = 5.65; LR− = 0.77.
Auscultation of mid-systolic click(s) is 11.1% sensitive and 98.5% specific for MVP; LR+ = 7.4; LR− = 0.90.

An association between MVP and panic disorder and agoraphobia does exist, for while the Framingham Offspring Study did not show an association between MVP and chest pain, palpitations, atrial arrhythmias, or ventricular arrhythmias, other studies did show an association with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
Increased height, decreased skin fold thickness, and decreased BMI are found disproportionately in patients with MVP compared with control patients.

Echocardiography has traditionally been considered the best diagnostic test for MVP. The diagnosis is made when one or both leaflets break the plane of the mitral annulus during systole, usually associated with inadequate leaflet approximation and therefore associated regurgitation.

Cardiac MRI has shows superiority to ECHO, and the MRI estimate of regurgitant volume, and regurgitant fraction, as it better predicts structural heart changes, In particular, late gadolinium enhancement and "dark papillary muscle sign" are predictors of myocardial fibrosis, left ventrciular dilation, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
,
In MVP, regurgitant volume is significant in mid to late systole on ECHO, whereas in secondary MR, the regurgitant volume is maximal in early systole, dropping in mid-systole.

Using surgical findings as the gold standard for comparison, 2D echocardiogram correlates 75% of the time for either leaflet; 3D echocardiogram correlates 87% in anterior leaflet prolapse and 93% in posterior leaflet prolapse. A

Three-dimensional (3D) echocardiography and transesophageal echocardiography are both superior to 2D echocardiography.
Although echocardiography is an acceptable modality for quantifying MR and making clinical decisions about management, cardiac MRI estimates LV function more accurately, and might evaluate severity of mitral regurgitation more reliably. By contrast, 2D ECHO underestimates LV end-diastolic volume, LV end-systolic volume.
MRI is equally accurate as 3D echo when evaluating mitral regurgitant fraction, but MRI is more accurate than echocardiography in assessing severity of MR.
Dehydration can create a false-positive echocardiogram for MVP.

Some have suggested that correction of magnesium deficiency reduces catecholamine levels and symptoms associated with MVP. However, this study included patients with "MVP Syndrome," a diagnosis that has since been debunked.
High BNP may distinguish asymptomatic patients with severe MR who would benefit from early MV repair, although it is not clear that other echo findings would predict the same result.

The detection of a mid or late systolic click is an important physical finding. Systolic clicks may be multiple and the click is sometimes followed by a crescendo-decrescendo murmur in late systole, best heard at the apex.

Performing one or more maneuvers on physical examination to decrease stroke volume, such as standing or performing a Valsalva maneuver, moves the click and murmur to earlier in systole. Squatting or releasing the Valsalva moves the click and murmur to later in systole.
A comprehensive evaluation of MVP may require an integrative approach utilizing multiple imaging modalities.

Echocardiogram or cardiac MRI are the diagnostic gold standard for MVP; 2D ECHO is the first-line diagnostic test. TEE and 3D transthoracic echocardiogram are more accurate than transthoracic 2D echocardiogram, but most cases can be evaluated initially with 2D transthoracic echocardiography.
Beta-blockers can be used to reduce adrenergic symptoms (but are not thought to be effective in attenuating severe mitral insufficiency from mitral valve prolapse). B

Long term outcomes are generally better when the mitral valve can be surgically repaired rather than replaced. Accordingly, MV repair is preferred as first-line management.
A
MV repair should be considered as soon as the patient begins to show secondary structural heart changes, especially decreasing right ventricular ejection fraction; atrial fibrillation, or symptoms. A

An older study showed enalapril for one year in patients with MVP with moderate to severe MR: reduced both MR and left ventricular (LV) diameter, and improved systolic LV function. Other studies have not reliably demonstrated improvement in cardiovascular outcomes in MVP patients treated with vasodilators.

The specific location of the MV prolapse, calcifications on the MV leaflets or annular ring, and the severity of MV annular dilatation may affect the feasibility and selection of MV repair or replacement options. Recent guidelines advocate for early surgical intervention for severe mitral regurgitation of MVP (even if the patient is asymptomatic) if repair is highly likely to be achieved in the operating room. Mitral valve surgery is indicated in patients with severe MR that are symptomatic or show echocardiographic criteria of LV dilation, LV dysfunction, reduced RV EF, or pulmonary hypertension.
MV repair after papillary muscle rupture yields good outcomes. Mitraclip, an artificial valve which can be placed via cardiac catheterization, is an option for patients with prohibitive surgical risk and appropriate anatomy. Mitraclip substantially improves both mortality and function in patients with high surgical risk and severe MR.
In a prospective, RCT, a population with mod-severe or severe MR and NYHA II-IVa HF and who were poor surgical candidates, Mitraclip replacement reduced all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stroke, and hospitalization for heart failure compared with medical management alone. Annuloplasty or repair of the annular leaflet alone have good outcomes in patients with severe mitral regurgitation and mitral valve prolapse with relatively low risk. In patients with MVP and MR due to MI, CABG alone is equivalent to CABG with MV repair at 12 months; there is no mortality nor quality of life benefit to performing MV repair of moderate ischemic MR, when CABG is required.

When all cardiac surgeries are compared for mortality benefit, isolated MV repair and isolated CABG are the surgeries showing a consistent mortality benefit, when performed for appropriate indications.

NICE guidelines state that evidence best supports performing MV repair by thoracoscopic-assisted surgery; both percutaneous MV annuloplasty and percutaneous MV repair of leaflets are considered experimental.

In 1 study, magnesium deficiency, with associated increased adrenergic activity, was present in 60% of highly symptomatic patients with MVP and only 5% of control patients. Magnesium repletion reduced catecholamine levels by 50% and improved symptoms in the deficient patients.
In children with MVP and poor exercise tolerance, coenzyme Q10 helped correct the activity-related decrease in LV function.

No treatment is recommended for athletes with MVP; in a case series of young athletes, 6% had MVP (according to the old criteria), one third had at least 1 recurrence of syncope, but none had a serious adverse outcome over 5 years of follow-up.
Any patient with hyperventilation, regardless of MVP status, benefits from learning appropriate breathing exercises.
Avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and tobacco use are recommended but clinical trials are lacking. C
Hospitalization is not required, except for cases of advancing arrhythmia or mitral valve regurgitation.
See "Surgery" section for criteria for referral to a surgeon for MV repair.

The prognosis is good for the great majority of patients with MVP; only those with severe MR or ventricular arrhtyhmias are at risk for increased mortality.*** Patients with valvular regurgitation should be monitored periodically for progressive disease. C

In a meta-analysis examining the risk of SCD, an increased risk of SCD (0.06 -0.08% SCDs per year in the incident population vs. 0.14% in population with MVP) occurred in patients with MVP. In addition to MVP, the presence of cardiac fibrosis, complex ventricular arrhythmias, and ST-T wave changes on EKG conferred additional risk for SCD. B A retrospective cohort study from the CDC found the greatest increase in risk of SCD among white women under age 44 years.
Key prognostic measures include right and left ventricular function, ventricular arrhythmias, severity of MR, and pulmonary pressures.
LV dysfunction is highly correlated with mortality in mitral regurgitation due to flail leaflets. A

Prognosis following MV repair is better in patients with fewer than 3 of the following: past history of heart failure; atrial fibrillation; pulmonary hypertension; increased LV end-systolic dimension; increased left atrial dimension; and reduced fractional shortening. B
There is no association between MVP and stroke in patients younger than 45 years. B
There is a lifetime increased risk of stroke, with RR 2.2.*
In patients 80 or older, survival after MV repair and replacement is 76.1% at 1 year, 67.7% at 3 years, and 56.5% at 5 years.
When performed for the proper indications, MV repair reduces mortality.

The MIDA-Q registry followed 8,187 patients with MVP and tracked them for mitral valve regurgitation and its progression, 50% continued with mild MR, 25% progressed to moderate and 25% progressed to severe MR.

Presence of MVP in pregnant women confers a greatly increased risk of adverse pregnancy and cardiac outcomes, including sudden cardiac death, arrhythmia, stroke, heart failure, coronary artery dissection, and higher obstetric risks including preterm delivery, preeclampsia, hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets syndrome.
MV surgery during pregnancy: standard outcomes for mother, with an increased risk of poor outcomes for fetus. Fetal survival especially poor with first-trimester surgery.
